---
name: chrome-devtools
description: Dirige um Chrome headless pelo MCP chrome-devtools-mcp para abrir páginas, clicar, ler console e rede, medir performance e salvar screenshots que o usuário vê no chat. Use quando a tarefa envolver um site ou app web real.
---

# Chrome DevTools

Use o MCP `chrome-devtools` para operar um navegador de verdade. Descubra as
ferramentas disponíveis antes do primeiro uso:

```
mcp_list { "server": "<id do servidor chrome-devtools>" }
```

O servidor sobe com `--slim`, então você tem apenas navegação, execução de
script e screenshot. Se precisar de rede, console ou trace, peça ao usuário para
reconfigurar o servidor sem `--slim`.

## Ordem obrigatória

1. `navigate_page` para abrir a URL.
2. `wait_for` pelo seletor ou texto que precisa existir. Nunca leia imediatamente
   após navegar.
3. `take_snapshot` para obter a árvore de acessibilidade com os `uid`.
4. Interaja pelos `uid`: `click`, `fill`, `press_key`.
5. Repita o snapshot após cada mudança de estado. `uid` antigo é inválido.

Uma ação por vez. Depois de cada ação, confirme com um novo snapshot em vez de
encadear cliques às cegas.

## Screenshots

Screenshot inline em base64 estoura o limite de resposta do Jeff. Sempre salve em
arquivo:

```
take_screenshot { "filePath": ".jeff/artifacts/<nome>.png" }
```

O Jeff lê imagens do projeto e mostra no chat automaticamente, então o usuário vê
exatamente o que você vê. Use nomes descritivos e não sobrescreva prints de
etapas diferentes.

## Regras

- Trabalhe em `localhost` e no que o usuário indicou. Não navegue para fora sem
  pedir.
- Nada de credenciais: se a página exigir login, pare e peça para o usuário
  conectar ou informar o acesso.
- Prefira snapshot a screenshot para decidir o próximo passo; screenshot é para o
  usuário, não para você.
- Se uma ação falhar, tire um snapshot antes de tentar de novo: o estado costuma
  ser diferente do que você assumiu.
- Relate a URL final e o que foi verificado.

# Jeff

![Jeff](packages/brand/assets/banner/jeff-banner-1500x500.png)

**Jeff** is a self-hosted workbench for machines you control. It brings code, databases, AI sessions and web apps into one place, with a workspace that feels close to VS Code and runs in your browser, on the desktop, or as a remote Android client.

Jeff is built for people who keep their own services, repositories and data on machines they control. There is no hosted account, no vendor backend and no telemetry.

## Public pages

- `/` — redirects to the workbench.
- `/app` — the workbench (sign-in required).

The installed server does not serve the landing page or documentation. The landing source lives in `landing/preview/` for separate local work only; it is not part of the installer, release or backend bundle.

## What it does

- Browse and edit project files with tabs, a file tree, unified search and live Git status. Source control changes and branch switching live in the Git modal.
- Run a real terminal attached to the server, with a draggable terminal height and working keyboard input.
- Debug with a focused agent: describe what happens and how it happens. The Jeff decides where to instrument, inserts temporary logs with its file tools, runs commands in a terminal you watch in real time and iterates until it isolates the cause. The debug view is only the conversation plus that terminal — no breakpoints or watches to set. The old Node/Python inspector studio is no longer mounted.
- Open repositories from a searchable repository picker; names are derived automatically. The picker can also create a new folder under an allowed workspace root and initialize it as a Git repository.
- Open projects as top-level tabs. Closing a project tab stops its terminal sessions and child processes without deleting the project.
- Use the real VS Code Material Icon Theme, stage/unstage/discard/commit and branch creation from configurable patterns in the Git modal, side-by-side diff tabs and Git blame for the current editor line.
- Search matches both file names and file content automatically with debounce, without pressing Enter.
- Ctrl+P opens and focuses the same unified search; conversations display streamed answers, tool activity, delegated agents and Markdown.
- Edit SQL table rows with primary-key safety.
- Connect to PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle, ClickHouse, Cassandra, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch and Neo4j, inspect schemas, run queries and inspect results.
- Run one Jeff per project with Jeff's native Rust harness, connecting directly to OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama or compatible model APIs.
- Configure the AI URL, API key and model in Settings → AI; API keys are encrypted at rest.
- Manage direct model connections and encrypted API keys from Settings → AI. The **Conexões de IA** tab adds named provider connections. Native MCP supports local stdio commands and remote Streamable HTTP endpoints with optional bearer tokens. Tool execution, delegation, cancellation, history and compaction belong to Jeff's backend.
- Enable editor autocomplete with an automatic lightweight model or a specific autocomplete model in Settings → AI.
- Add server folders as workspace roots in Settings → Workspace, without Docker bind mounts.
- Keep self-hosted and external web apps in their own tabs, including pages that block iframes, through a server-side preview proxy.
- Switch between projects without losing the state of the current one.
- Use the same backend from the browser, desktop app and Tauri Android client.
- Get an in-app toast when a new release is available; the button updates the server and reloads connected web clients.
- Receive in-app AI response notifications and Android push notifications through Firebase Cloud Messaging, including when the app is closed.
- Download the next desktop installer directly from the update toast, with checksum verification. Windows publishes both NSIS and MSI installers, and the toast prefers NSIS.
- Run desktop local mode with optional LAN sharing, show a one-time pairing QR, and open the same local workspace from the Android app by scanning it.
- Use a native-titlebar-only desktop shell with a VS Code-style header containing menus, project and branch selectors, editor status, and an agent rail.
- Personalize the web app with light/dark themes, the Jeff blue accent, sidebar width, editor and terminal typography, tab styles, and three global icon sets: Material, Phosphor Fill and Remix Fill. The icon choice applies to the entire interface and the file tree. Drag the sidebar, agent dock and terminal edges to resize them.

## Repository layout

```text
backend/           Rust API; app composition, platform and feature modules
web/               React workbench; app, features and shared UI
desktop/           Tauri desktop entrypoint and packaging
mobile/            Tauri Android entrypoint, Kotlin and push integration
landing/site/      Published static landing page
landing/preview/   Independent React landing preview
packages/launcher/ Shared native launcher interface
packages/native/   Shared Tauri runtime source
packages/brand/    Brand assets and BrandMark
packages/ui/       Shared React UI primitives
packages/icons/    Shared icon components
deploy/            Docker Compose
```

The backend embeds only the application. The landing page is never installed, embedded, released or served by the Jeff server.

Asset copies (Monaco, file icons, `onig.wasm`, brand) happen in each Vite config, so `npm run dev`/`npm run build` need no pre-step. Release versioning and component detection are inline steps in `.github/workflows/release.yml`.

## Architecture

```text
Browser (React)                     Tauri (desktop + Android)
        │                                    │
        └──────────── HTTPS / WSS ───────────┘
                          │
                    jeff (Rust)
        ├── auth and sessions
        ├── projects and workspace files
        ├── terminal (PTY over WebSocket)
        ├── database gateway
        ├── native agent runtime and direct model providers
        └── web target registry
                          │
        repositories · PostgreSQL · SQLite · MySQL · model APIs
```

The Rust server is the only component that touches repositories, database credentials and shells. Clients are thin: they render tabs and stream data. The browser build is embedded in the Rust binary; desktop and Android clients use the same API. Desktop local mode embeds the Rust server in the Tauri process itself, so no separate server process is started.

## Security

- Passwords use Argon2id; sessions are stored as token hashes.
- Browser sessions use `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite=Strict` cookies when `JEFF_SECURE_COOKIES=true`.
- Cookie-authenticated mutations require a double-submit CSRF token.
- Login and API endpoints have per-client rate limits.
- `X-Forwarded-For` is only trusted from loopback or the CIDRs in `JEFF_TRUSTED_PROXIES`.
- Model and MCP credentials are managed by the backend and are not exposed to the browser or model prompts.
- API responses use `Cache-Control: no-store` and responses are protected against framing.

## Run it

### Requirements

- Rust stable (1.90+ recommended)
- Node.js 22+
- SQLite is embedded through SQLx
- Linux, macOS or a Linux container
- Docker and Docker Compose v2, optional

### Development

```sh
cp .env.example .env
cargo run --manifest-path backend/Cargo.toml --bin jeff
```

In another terminal:

```sh
npm install
npm run dev:web
```

Landing source, separately (not part of the installable app):

```sh
npm run dev:landing
```

App: `http://localhost:5173/app/`. Landing source: `http://localhost:5174/`.

### Production build

```sh
make build
./bin/jeff
```

`make build` builds `web` and embeds it into the Rust binary. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8787`.

### One-command install

On a Debian/Ubuntu server or LXC:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/ferforastieri/jeff/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sudo sh
```

The installer creates the `jeff` user, installs the binary, creates a systemd
service, generates the first password and starts Jeff on port `8787`. It also
installs the root-owned update helper used by the in-app update toast.

The server installer can also provision a development environment on the
server, where Jeff's terminal and tools actually run:

```sh
curl -fsSL .../install.sh | sudo sh -s -- --components git,node,pnpm,rust,go,python
```

Use `--components all` or `--no-components`. The desktop launcher offers the
same optional tool selection for local workspaces; remote desktop, web and
mobile clients never install toolchains on the client machine.

### Releases

Every successful CI run on `main` publishes the next GitHub release
automatically. The version bump follows Conventional Commits across the commits
since the latest release:

- `fix:` — patch (`0.8.10` → `0.8.11`)
- `feat:` — small feature, minor (`0.8.10` → `0.9.0`)
- `feat!:` or `BREAKING CHANGE:` — large feature, major (`0.8.10` → `1.0.0`)
- other commit types — patch

The pipeline creates the tag, builds the server, APK and desktop installers, and
publishes the release. It never deploys to a server by itself.

Remote servers expose an update toast when a newer release exists. Clicking
**Update** writes an authenticated update request; the root-owned helper runs
the same `install.sh` release flow, checks health and rolls back on failure.

On the Android APK, the same action also asks Android's DownloadManager for the
latest signed APK. The first APK that contains this downloader must be installed
manually from the release; subsequent updates can download the next APK from the
toast. Installing the downloaded APK still requires the normal Android prompt.

### Desktop

Install the Windows or Linux package from the [latest release](https://github.com/ferforastieri/jeff/releases/latest). Desktop local mode embeds the Rust Jeff server and asks for a workspace folder; server mode asks only for a URL on first use and reconnects to the last server on later launches. The launcher also offers an optional development-environment installer for Git, Node.js, pnpm, Rust, Go and Python. The local backend uses the app data directory for SQLite and its generated admin password.

The desktop and Android entrypoints share `packages/launcher/` and `packages/native/`; Android remains remote-only and does not compile the embedded server. Windows ships a Jeff-branded NSIS installer (per-user or per-machine, directory and shortcut choices, Portuguese/English/Spanish, MIT license) and an equivalent WiX MSI, both with the current brand artwork.

### Docker

```sh
JEFF_WORKSPACES_HOST=/srv/workspaces docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml up --build
```

Mount the repositories you want to expose under `/workspaces` and keep `JEFF_DATA_DIR` on a persistent volume. The container runs as UID 1000; make sure the mounted workspace is writable by that user, or adjust the Compose `user:` setting.

### Desktop and Android

Signed Android APKs are published on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/ferforastieri/jeff/releases). They are remote-only.

The Tauri entrypoints live in `desktop/` and `mobile/`. The desktop can connect to a Jeff server or run the embedded local Rust backend. On Android it is a remote-only client: the WebView connects to the Jeff server URL configured on the launcher, and no local server or terminal runs on the phone.

For Android development, install JDK 21, Android SDK 36 and NDK 28.2, then:

```sh
npm ci
cd mobile
npm run icons
npm run tauri -- android build --debug --apk --target aarch64
```

The generated Android project is committed in `src-tauri/gen/android`; release signing reads the `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_*` environment variables. The Firebase client config (`app/google-services.json`) is not in git: CI writes it from the `GOOGLE_SERVICES_JSON` secret, and local Android builds expect a copy of that file at the same path (ignored by git). Use LAN, VPN or Tailscale for the server URL; do not expose the server directly to the internet.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `JEFF_ADDR` | `127.0.0.1:8787` | HTTP listen address |
| `JEFF_DATA_DIR` | `./data` | SQLite, master key and runtime data |
| `JEFF_WORKSPACES` | `/workspaces` | Colon-separated roots that projects may use |
| `JEFF_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | generated on first run | Initial admin password |
| `JEFF_SECURE_COOKIES` | `false` | Require HTTPS for browser sessions; the installer sets `true` |
| `JEFF_TRUSTED_PROXIES` | empty | Comma-separated proxy IPs/CIDRs allowed to supply `X-Forwarded-For` |
| `JEFF_FIREBASE_CREDENTIALS_FILE` | empty | Firebase service-account JSON used by the server for Android push |
| `JEFF_FIREBASE_PROJECT_ID` | service-account project | Firebase project ID for Cloud Messaging |
| `JEFF_WEB_DIR` | embedded build | Serve a web build from disk in development |
| `JEFF_UPDATE_REPO` | `ferforastieri/jeff` | GitHub repository used by the in-app update check |
| `JEFF_DEV_COMPONENTS` | empty | Server installer only: `git,node,pnpm,rust,go,python`, `all`, or `none` |

## Security

Jeff can read files, open shells and reach databases. Treat it as a remote administration tool:

- bind it to localhost, LAN or a VPN;
- put TLS in front of it;
- use a strong password and keep the data directory private;
- do not publish it on the public internet.

## Desktop

The client lives in `desktop/` and uses Tauri 2. The same project builds Windows and Linux installers, with a Tauri Android target for mobile. Server mode accepts any Jeff server URL; local mode embeds the Rust backend in the Tauri process, asks for a workspace folder, serves the UI on loopback (or on the LAN when phone pairing is enabled), and shuts the backend down when the app exits. # Jeff Client

Tauri 2 Windows/Linux entrypoint. The launcher UI is in `packages/launcher/`
and the shared Rust runtime is in `packages/native/`. Android has its own
entrypoint in `mobile/`.

## Modes

- **Server:** asks only for a Jeff server URL, validates `/api/health`, then opens the normal Jeff web app in a native window.
- **Local (desktop only):** asks for a workspace folder, starts the embedded Rust Jeff backend, authenticates the embedded WebView through a one-time pairing code, and opens the local workbench. Closing the workspace window stops the backend and its terminal sessions. Local mode listens only on loopback unless **Acessar pelo celular nesta rede** is enabled; then it also listens on the LAN and shows a QR code that pairs the Android app in one scan.

The local backend stores SQLite, the generated local admin password and master key under the app data directory. It does not use or expose a remote server. The workspace folder is passed as `JEFF_WORKSPACES`, so its projects are the local working set.

On Windows the backend uses ConPTY for terminals; on Linux it uses a Unix PTY. The remote server page runs inside the system WebView (WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux) and receives no Tauri IPC capability.

Android is remote-only. The Android app hides local mode, connects to a Jeff server URL, and can scan the desktop pairing QR from the launcher.

## Development

From the repository root:

```bash
npm install
make build
cd desktop
npm run tauri dev
```

For local mode, the Rust Jeff server is embedded in the Tauri process. The launcher picks a folder and starts it on loopback, or on the LAN when phone pairing is enabled; no `bin/jeff` sidecar is needed. The launcher also offers an optional development-environment installer (Git, Node.js, pnpm, Rust, Go and Python).

## Build

```bash
cd desktop
npm run tauri -- build
```

Linux requires WebKitGTK/GTK development packages. Windows requires WebView2 and the MSVC Rust toolchain. The Linux and Windows CI jobs build the Rust server as part of the Tauri binary. Android does not compile the desktop server crate.

Windows publishes both formats: the NSIS installer offers per-user or per-machine installation, a custom directory, Start Menu and desktop shortcuts, a language selector (Portuguese, English, Spanish), the MIT license and a run-after-finish checkbox. MSI keeps the same artwork and license for environments that deploy MSI. Regenerate the installer bitmaps after brand changes:

```bash
python3 -m pip install --user pillow
python3 desktop/scripts/installer-images.py
```

The script reads the mascot and wordmark from `packages/brand/assets` and writes the 24-bit BMP files Tauri expects.

## Android

From the repository root:

```bash

cd mobile
npm run tauri -- android init
npm run tauri -- android build --debug --apk --target aarch64
```

Requires JDK 21, Android SDK 36 and NDK 28.2. The generated `src-tauri/gen/android` project is intentionally not committed; `tauri android init` recreates it. The Android client is remote-only.

# Shared native runtime

`src/lib.rs` is compiled by the small entrypoints in `desktop/src-tauri` and
`mobile/src-tauri`. Each application owns its Tauri configuration, capabilities,
build script and distribution assets. This keeps the Rust command handlers and
local-server lifecycle in a single implementation without another process.

`tauri::generate_context!()` uses the consuming entrypoint's Cargo manifest.
The Android target excludes local-server functionality and its backend dependency.

## What it does

- One Jeff per task or several Jeffs in a group. Each runs in its own session with shared task history.
- Router picks 0–2 Jeffs for a message; explicit `@handle` mentions win; `todos` calls everyone; a Jeff can delegate or mention another.
- Engines: OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex. Others listed but not wired.
- Models: OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Groq, Mistral, xAI, Ollama or a company gateway.
- Permissions: Plan (read only), Ask (approval before changes), YOLO (allowed tools run without prompting).
- Tools: files, shell, Git, MCP, skills, memory, artifacts, images, audio, questions and approvals.
- Workbench: project explorer/editor, terminal, source control, databases, debug, web apps and previews.
- Files: upload, edit and stream downloads of any size.

## Install (Linux, root)

```bash
# 1. install binary + systemd service
curl -fsSL https://github.com/ferforastieri/jeff/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sudo sh -s -- --no-components

# 2. review the generated environment
sudo sed -n '1,120p' /etc/jeff/jeff.env

# 3. start and enable
sudo systemctl enable --now jeff

# 4. verify
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/health
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/version
```

Expected minimum configuration:

```env
JEFF_ADDR=0.0.0.0:8787
JEFF_DATA_DIR=/var/lib/jeff
JEFF_WORKSPACES=/srv/jeff/workspaces
JEFF_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<strong-password>
JEFF_SECURE_COOKIES=false
JEFF_TRUSTED_PROXIES=
```

Use `JEFF_SECURE_COOKIES=true` behind HTTPS. Set `JEFF_TRUSTED_PROXIES` to the reverse proxy IP/CIDR. The frontend is at `/app`; login uses the `jeff_session` cookie. Data lives in `JEFF_DATA_DIR/jeff.db`; the master key is `JEFF_DATA_DIR/master.key`. Back up both together.

## Docker

```bash
cd jeff

```

## Requirements

- Linux x86_64/arm64 server (or the desktop app on macOS/Linux/Windows).
- Port 8787 free (or set `JEFF_ADDR`).
- Git; Node/pnpm and Rust only when building from source.
- A model connection (API key, gateway or local Ollama) for the Jeffs.

## First Jeff

1. Settings → Connections: connect a model provider and test it.
2. Use the `+` button: it lists every Git repository under the allowed workspace roots. Pick one; Jeff creates and opens the project if needed.
3. Create a Jeff: choose a profile (Jeff, Leo, Nico, Nova, Bia, Pia, Atlas, Rafa) or start from zero. Set name, handle, role, prompt, model, engine, effort and tools.
4. Choose permissions: Plan, Ask or YOLO.
5. Open a task and write. Mention `@handle`, attach images/files, or record audio. History stays with the task.

## Groups and ordering

- A message without a mention goes through the router; it selects 0–2 Jeffs, or everyone when asked.
- An explicit mention always wins.
- Each selected Jeff runs in its own session with the shared task history.
- A new message while a run is active cancels the previous run, waits for it to end and inserts the new user message after the previous output.

## Tools, MCP and approvals

- File, shell, Git and artifact tools run through the Jeff gateway.
- Settings → Connections → MCPs: configure servers and select which Jeff can use each one. The agent calls `mcp_list` and `mcp_call`.
- Approval modes: Plan (read only), Ask (approval before mutations), YOLO (allowed tools run).
- Skills are reusable recipes; memory stores durable project facts. Both are exposed to the agent.

## Workbench

- Explorer/editor, file upload and streaming download.
- Source control: status, diffs, stage, commit, branches, blame, discard.
- Terminal per project.
- Databases: Postgres, MySQL, SQLite connections, schema and queries.
- Debug: breakpoints, console, variables.
- Web apps and previews with logs.

## Attachments

- Drag and drop images or use the attach button.
- Up to 6 attachments and 8 MB total per message; the run endpoint accepts a 32 MB body.
- OpenCode receives images as real `--file` attachments.
- Audio can be transcribed by the browser; otherwise it is attached as a file.

## Update

- Settings → Harness: update OpenCode (`opencode upgrade`), Claude Code (`claude update`) or Codex (`npm install -g @openai/codex@latest`).
- OpenCode must be 2.2.6 or newer; older versions lose MCP tools on the first turn.
- Re-run the installer to update the Jeff binary; the app also exposes releases.
- Hard refresh (`Ctrl+Shift+R`) after a frontend update.

## Troubleshooting

- Agent shows only `skill` / no tools: update OpenCode to 2.2.6+.
- `mcp_list` 401: the MCP token expired; update it in Connections.
- `mcp_list` “not selected”: the server name/id does not belong to that Jeff; use the exact name from the prompt.
- Image send does nothing: update the app, hard refresh, keep attachments under 8 MB total; the route accepts 32 MB.
- Download “not available”: ensure the reverse proxy forwards `/api/projects/*/raw` and does not buffer the stream. Jeff streams any size.
- 401 behind HTTPS: set `JEFF_SECURE_COOKIES=true` and `JEFF_TRUSTED_PROXIES`.
- Port busy: `ss -ltnp | grep 8787`, then change `JEFF_ADDR`.

## For AI agents

Goal: install and verify Jeff on a Linux server.

```bash

curl -fsSL https://github.com/ferforastieri/jeff/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sudo sh -s -- --no-components

# 2. configure
sudo sed -n '1,120p' /etc/jeff/jeff.env
# edit JEFF_ADDR, JEFF_WORKSPACES, JEFF_ADMIN_PASSWORD, JEFF_SECURE_COOKIES

# 3. start
sudo systemctl enable --now jeff

# 4. verify
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/health
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/version
```

Rules:

- Do not invent paths; use the values above or the ones already present in `/etc/jeff/jeff.env`.
- Do not print or commit secrets. `JEFF_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, API keys and `master.key` are secret.
- Back up `JEFF_DATA_DIR/jeff.db` and `JEFF_DATA_DIR/master.key` together.
- If a command fails, show the exact output and stop; do not fake a successful install.
- After install, report the URL, version, data directory and where the database and master key live.

# Jeff

Jeff is a self-hosted workbench for machines you control. It runs on your server and provides a browser client and a Tauri Android client.

## Core facts

- Single-tenant, self-hosted, MIT licensed.
- Go backend with embedded React web client.
- Android client: Kotlin/Jetpack Compose.
- Tabs: code editor, database console, native AI chat, terminal, web app.
- Browser editor: Monaco.
- Android editor: CodeMirror 6 in a local WebView.
- Web app tabs: Android WebView; browser iframe with external fallback.
- The server owns files, PTYs, database credentials and AI sessions.
- Clients are thin and connect over HTTPS/WSS.
- Not a VS Code fork, not a multi-tenant SaaS, not a complete DBeaver replacement.

## Architecture

Browser (React) and Android (Compose) connect to the Go server over HTTPS/WSS.

The Go server provides:
- authentication and sessions;
- projects and workspace files;
- ripgrep search and git status;
- PTY terminals;
- SQL and NoSQL database gateway;
- native agent runtime;
- web target registry;
- embedded web build.

Repositories, databases and agent execution remain on the server. Database credentials are encrypted with AES-GCM and never sent to clients.

## Install

One command (Debian/Ubuntu/LXC):

    curl -fsSL https://github.com/ferforastieri/jeff/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sudo sh

Docker:

    git clone https://github.com/ferforastieri/jeff.git
    cd jeff
    JEFF_WORKSPACES_HOST=/srv/workspaces \
    JEFF_ADMIN_PASSWORD='strong-password' \
    docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml up --build

Binary:

    make build
    JEFF_WORKSPACES=/srv/workspaces \
    JEFF_ADMIN_PASSWORD='strong-password' \
    ./bin/jeff

Open:

    http://127.0.0.1:8787/

Landing page: `/`
Application: `/app`
Docs: `/docs.html`
Machine-readable docs: `/llms.txt`

## Android

Download the signed APK from GitHub Releases. Debug APKs are not published.

Local development only:

    cd android
    ./gradlew assembleDebug

On first launch, enter the Jeff server URL, username and password. Use LAN, VPN or Tailscale. Do not expose Jeff directly to the internet.

## Configuration

JEFF_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8787
JEFF_DATA_DIR=./data
JEFF_WORKSPACES=/workspaces
JEFF_ADMIN_PASSWORD=
JEFF_SECURE_COOKIES=false
JEFF_BUILD_ID=
JEFF_WEB_DIR=

JEFF_WORKSPACES is a colon-separated list of existing directories. Projects must be inside these roots.


AI provider accounts and API keys can be connected from Settings → AI → Conexões de IA in the web or Android client. The same screen lists every model provider available to the agent.

The MCP tab in Settings → AI manages local and remote Model Context Protocol servers, including OAuth authentication, connect/disconnect and removal. Editor autocomplete can use an automatic lightweight model or a specific model selected in Settings → AI.

## Databases

SQL/CQL drivers: PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, SQL Server, Oracle, ClickHouse, Cassandra. Search/graph: Elasticsearch, Neo4j.

DSN examples:

    PostgreSQL   postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db?sslmode=disable
    MySQL        user:pass@tcp(host:3306)/db
    SQLite       /path/to/database.db
    SQL Server   sqlserver://user:pass@host:1433?database=db
    Oracle       oracle://user:pass@host:1521/service
    ClickHouse   clickhouse://user:pass@host:9000/db

MongoDB query format:

    {"database":"app","collection":"users","filter":{},"limit":100}

MongoDB aggregation uses `pipeline` instead of `filter`.

Redis query format: a Redis command string.

    GET session:42
    HGETALL user:1
    SCAN 0 COUNT 100

Read-only profiles reject writes. SQL profiles use read-only drivers/queries where supported.

SQL table tabs support row editing when the table has a primary key and the profile is not read-only. Updates use the primary key in the WHERE clause.

Cassandra uses CQL. Elasticsearch accepts JSON `{index, body}`. Neo4j accepts Cypher.

## Native agent runtime

Jeff executes agents in Rust and connects directly to OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages, Ollama and compatible APIs. Configure URL, API key and model in Settings → AI. Credentials are encrypted at rest. No installed agent service or CLI is used.

The backend owns sessions, tools, cancellation, approvals, delegation, token budgets and incremental compaction. Original history remains searchable. The browser follows SSE events and reconnects through snapshots. Provider errors do not switch models. MCP supports stdio and Streamable HTTP.

## Updates

Web: polls `/api/version`. When `buildId` changes, a toast appears; clicking reloads and clears caches.

Android: checks the latest GitHub release for an APK. When a newer tag exists with an APK asset, a toast appears; clicking downloads the APK and opens the Android installer. Android requires the final install confirmation. Release builds use a signing keystore when the Android secrets are configured; otherwise the workflow publishes a debug APK.

## Security

- Bind to localhost, LAN or VPN.
- Put TLS in front.
- Use a strong password.
- Login is rate-limited.
- Session tokens are opaque and stored hashed.
- Project paths are restricted with symlink escape checks.
- Database credentials are encrypted at rest.
- Treat Jeff as remote administration.
